title: Constitutional Writ Remedies — Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto

content.overview: Articles 32 and 226 empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. These writs are the primary constitutional remedies for controlling administrative and other public action.
content.glance: Identify the wrong and the appropriate writ; state the conditions for each writ; address maintainability (standing, alternative remedy, delay); formulate the precise relief.
content.study: Habeas corpus secures personal liberty against unlawful detention. Mandamus commands a public authority to perform a public duty. Prohibition and certiorari control excess of jurisdiction by inferior courts or tribunals (prohibition prospectively, certiorari to quash). Quo warranto challenges usurpation of a public office. High Court jurisdiction under Article 226 is broader than Supreme Court jurisdiction under Article 32 (which is primarily for fundamental rights). Current-law framing: ground the analysis in Articles 32 and 226 and the specific writ conditions.

sections.heading: Habeas Corpus
sections.body: Secures release from unlawful detention; the detaining authority must justify the detention.

sections.heading: Mandamus
sections.body: Commands performance of a public duty by a public authority; requires a clear legal right and corresponding duty.

sections.heading: Prohibition and Certiorari
sections.body: Control jurisdictional excess by inferior courts/tribunals; prohibition restrains, certiorari quashes.

sections.heading: Quo Warranto
sections.body: Challenges the legality of a person’s claim to a public office.

sections.heading: Maintainability
sections.body: Standing, alternative remedy, delay and clean hands regulate the discretionary grant of writ relief.

provisions.title: Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for fundamental rights

examples.title: Mandamus for statutory duty
examples.body: A statute imposes a clear duty on an authority to decide an application within a time. The authority refuses to act. Mandamus may compel performance of the duty.

examples.title: Certiorari to quash
examples.body: A tribunal decides without jurisdiction or in breach of natural justice. Certiorari is the appropriate writ to quash the decision.

hypotheticals.question: Can mandamus compel a purely discretionary act?
hypotheticals.analysis: Mandamus can compel the authority to exercise the discretion according to law; it does not ordinarily dictate the particular outcome of a true discretion.

hypotheticals.question: Is alternative remedy an absolute bar to Article 226?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. It is a rule of practice; exceptional circumstances may justify direct writ intervention.

distinctions.title: Prohibition vs certiorari
distinctions.left: Restrains proceedings in excess of jurisdiction (prospective)
distinctions.right: Quashes a decision already made in excess of jurisdiction (retrospective)

distinctions.title: Article 32 vs Article 226
distinctions.right: High Court; broader (rights and other legal injuries)

misconceptions.trap: Every administrative grievance supports a writ.
misconceptions.correction: The appropriate writ conditions, standing, alternative remedy and delay must be satisfied.

misconceptions.trap: Mandamus can dictate the merits outcome of every discretion.
misconceptions.correction: It compels performance of duty or lawful exercise of discretion; it does not ordinarily substitute the court’s preferred outcome.

cases.name: Tata Cellular v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Courts exercise supervisory jurisdiction; remedies are framed to correct legality defects.
cases.holding: Review standards and remedial approach applied.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a writ-remedies problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the wrong. II. Select the appropriate writ and state its conditions. III. Address maintainability. IV. Formulate precise relief.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Facts; writ chosen with conditions; maintainability; precise prayer.

bareActPointers: Parent statute creating the duty or tribunal
examTips: Match the wrong to the correct writ.
